---
title: "Bayesian estimation"
subtitle: "Priors, posteriors and a replication"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The fits run once, in companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing.R; the page reads
# their summaries and a thinned set of draws
counts <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_counts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
draws <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
summ <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dx <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_diagnostics.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sens <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_sensitivity.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ppc <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/bayes_housing_ppc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
replication <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_replication.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
ref_low <- ref$b_pp - stats::qt(0.975, ref$df) * ref$se_pp
ref_high <- ref$b_pp + stats::qt(0.975, ref$df) * ref$se_pp
repl_row <- datawizard::data_filter(replication, population == "replies", authorities == "all")

# One row of the summaries for each result quoted on the page
prior_weak <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "prior_weak", quantity == "gap")
prior_scep <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "prior_sceptical", quantity == "gap")
prior_white <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "prior_weak", quantity == "white_share")
orig_weak <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "original_weak", quantity == "gap")
orig_scep <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "original_sceptical", quantity == "gap")
coef_weak <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "original_weak", quantity == "coef")
repl_alone <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "replication_alone", quantity == "gap")
repl_upd <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "replication_updated", quantity == "gap")
joint_orig <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "joint_common", quantity == "gap_original")
joint_diff <- datawizard::data_filter(summ, model == "joint_separate", quantity == "difference")
sens_weak <- datawizard::data_filter(sens, model == "original_weak")
sens_scep <- datawizard::data_filter(sens, model == "original_sceptical")
sens_upd <- datawizard::data_filter(sens, model == "replication_updated")
ppc_common <- datawizard::data_filter(ppc, model == "joint_common", study == "original")
```

The gap stated in the claim of the Housing and racial bias case study is estimated in this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) by Bayesian methods, and the module also asks what these methods add in a case of this kind. The case study rests on a field experiment in which the original authors emailed public housing authorities in the United States from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant, finding that replies to the Hispanic names opened with the sender's name less often, by a gap of about 20 percentage points among the replies [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. A preregistered replication conducted for the SCORE replicability study with new names and more authorities found no significant gap, and the two studies are presented in full on the [background page](../background.qmd). It is in a situation of this kind, in which a significant result from a study of moderate size is followed by a larger replication that finds nothing, that the habits of Bayesian estimation arguably earn their keep. The estimate becomes a distribution about which direct probability statements can be made, and what was believed before the data has to be written down and checked. The replication then enters as new data revising the earlier estimate, while the plausibility of the original result can be judged against what a study of its size could find. The module follows the work of Andrew Gelman and Richard McElreath and relies on brms, which fits Bayesian regression models in R through the Stan language [@Burkner2017BrmsPackageBayesian].

The models were fitted once, in the script `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing.R`, since a Bayesian fit takes longer than a page should take to build. The page presents the code of each model and reads the summaries and the draws written by that script.

## 1. A model of the greetings {#sec-model}

The comparison examined here is the reference specification of the course, which sets Hispanic against white names among the replies that carry a greeting code, with no covariates. Since the outcome of each reply is 0 or 1 and the model has a single binary predictor, everything that the data say about the outcome is contained in four counts, namely the number of replies to each group and the number of those replies that opened with the name. As the replication published no file that the course may copy, its counts are recovered in the script from the shares and the total number of replies reported in `display_replication.csv`. These recovered counts agree with the 721 replies to Hispanic and 763 to white aliases in the de-identified replication file.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "The replies to Hispanic and white names that carry a greeting code, and those that opened with the name of the sender, in the original experiment and in the replication. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_counts.csv`."
#| echo: false
counts |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    Study = dplyr::if_else(study == "original", "Original experiment, 2014", "Replication, 2020"),
    Names = dplyr::if_else(hisp == 1, "Hispanic", "white"),
    Share = insight::format_value(k / n, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Study", "Names", Replies = "n", `Greeted by name` = "k", "Share")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:5, align = "r")
```

A binomial model treats the greetings in each group as a count out of the replies, with the probability of a greeting linked to the names by a logistic regression. This is the same model as the logistic regression presented in the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd#sec-logit), fitted to the four counts instead of to the `r sum(counts$n[counts$study == "original"])` replies one by one, and it yields the same answer. In brms the number of trials is written beside the count, and `0 + Intercept` retains the intercept as the log-odds of a greeting for the white names, so that its prior can be stated on that scale.

```{r}
#| label: brms-model
#| eval: false
original <- datawizard::data_filter(counts, study == "original")
fit_original <- brms::brm(
  k | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + hisp, family = stats::binomial(), data = original,
  prior = c(brms::prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
            brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "hisp")),
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 20261105, backend = "cmdstanr"
)
```

## 2. Priors and what they imply {#sec-priors}

A Bayesian model requires a prior distribution for each parameter, and both parameters of this model lie on the log-odds scale, which few people can read directly. McElreath illustrates why the scale matters with a logistic regression of his own, in which a prior of normal(0, 10) on the intercept, vague as it looks, puts "most of the probability mass ... near zero and one", since "[a] flat prior in the logit space is not a flat prior in the outcome probability space" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, p. 328]. The intercept of the present model takes his normal(0, 1.5), which is nearly flat on the probability scale. A prior is called weakly informative in *Bayesian Data Analysis* "if it is proper but is set up so that the information it does provide is intentionally weaker than whatever actual prior knowledge is available" [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, p. 55], and both priors on the intercept, as well as the first prior on the gap, are of that kind.

The gap requires more thought, and the module compares two priors for it, both centred on no gap. The weakly informative prior, normal(0, 1), allows coefficients of about ±2 on the log-odds scale, and since near a share of one half a coefficient of 2 moves a probability by up to half its range, this prior rules out almost nothing that a field experiment could produce. The sceptical prior, normal(0, 0.25), describes a reader who expects a name to change the tone of a reply by about as much as it changed whether a reply came at all. Given that the reply gap between white and Hispanic names in the same experiment was 4.8 points, this reader gives gaps of more than ten points little credence. As the reply gap comes from another outcome of the experiment, whether a reply came at all, the prior uses none of the greetings to which the model is then fitted. Neither prior is meant as the right one, and between them the two priors bracket a reader who has no view and a reader who doubts large effects of a name, leaving to section 3 the question of how far each reader would be moved by the data.

What a prior implies on the scale of the claim is seldom obvious, and the way to find out is to simulate from the prior before the data enter. The literature on workflow calls this a prior predictive check, "a way to assess the pre-data implications of a generative model", which is useful "because parameter distributions interact with the data model to produce implied predictions" and "it can be difficult to intuit the consequences of prior choices" [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow, p. 89]. When `sample_prior = "only"` is set, brms fits the model with the likelihood switched off, and marginaleffects converts the resulting draws into the gap in percentage points, the predicted share of greetings for a Hispanic name minus that for a white name. Since the number of trials is set to 1 in `newdata`, each prediction is a probability rather than a count.

```{r}
#| label: brms-prior
#| eval: false
fit_prior <- brms::brm(
  k | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + hisp, family = stats::binomial(), data = original,
  prior = c(brms::prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
            brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "hisp")),
  sample_prior = "only", chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 20261105, backend = "cmdstanr"
)
marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_prior, variables = "hisp", newdata = tibble::tibble(hisp = 0L, n = 1L))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "The prior predictive distributions of the model: the share of replies to white names that open with the name of the sender (left) and the gap between Hispanic and white names (right), under the weakly informative prior normal(0, 1) and the sceptical prior normal(0, 0.25) for the gap. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_draws.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Left: two nearly flat densities of the white share across 0 to 100%, falling only near the ends. Right: the weakly informative prior gives a broad hump from about −40 to +40 points, and the sceptical prior a narrow peak within about ±10 points."
draws |>
  datawizard::data_filter(model %in% c("prior_weak", "prior_sceptical")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    prior = dplyr::if_else(model == "prior_weak", "weakly informative", "sceptical"),
    panel = dplyr::if_else(quantity == "white_share", "share greeted by name, white names (%)",
                           "gap, Hispanic minus white names (points)")
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(value, colour = prior)) +
  ggplot2::geom_density(linewidth = 0.8, bounds = c(-100, 100)) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(panel), scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`weakly informative` = "#0e3b6a", sceptical = "#8c5a10"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "prior density") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Before the data enter, both models expect a share of greetings for the white names anywhere between `r insight::format_value(prior_white$q025, digits = 0)`% and `r insight::format_value(prior_white$q975, digits = 0)`% (the central 95% of the prior), which says only that a share is a share. The weakly informative prior places 95% of its gaps between `r insight::format_value(prior_weak$q025, digits = 0, style_negative = "minus")` and +`r insight::format_value(prior_weak$q975, digits = 0)` points, a range containing every gap on the specification curve of the case study as well as the results of both studies. The sceptical prior, by contrast, confines the same share of its gaps to between `r insight::format_value(prior_scep$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` and +`r insight::format_value(prior_scep$q975, digits = 1)` points, giving a gap of more than 10 points to the disadvantage of the Hispanic names a probability of only `r insight::format_value(prior_scep$p_beyond_10, digits = 3)`. The two ranges express the two readers in numbers, and the check shows that neither prior places its mass on outcomes that no experiment could produce.

## 3. The posterior of the gap {#sec-posterior}

Once the likelihood is switched on, the same call of `avg_comparisons()` on the fitted model returns the posterior distribution of the gap, whose 4,000 draws are returned by `marginaleffects::get_draws()`. Each draw represents one value of the gap compatible with the data and the prior, and every summary of the posterior is a summary of these draws.

```{r}
#| label: brms-posterior
#| eval: false
gap <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit_original, variables = "hisp",
                                        newdata = tibble::tibble(hisp = 0L, n = 1L))
gap_draws <- marginaleffects::get_draws(gap, shape = "long")
bayestestR::describe_posterior(100 * gap_draws$draw, ci = 0.95, ci_method = "ETI")
```

Under the weakly informative prior the posterior median of the gap is `r insight::format_value(orig_weak$median, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, with a 95% credible interval from `r insight::format_value(orig_weak$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(orig_weak$q975, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`, while the coefficient on the log-odds scale has a median of `r insight::format_value(coef_weak$median, digits = 3, style_negative = "minus")`. The reference specification of the course, the difference in proportions with HC2 errors, yields `r insight::format_value(ref$b_pp, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, with a 95% confidence interval from `r insight::format_value(ref_low, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(ref_high, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`. The two estimates agree closely, because a prior this weak is outweighed by `r sum(counts$n[counts$study == "original"])` replies, and the posterior lies about a point nearer zero because the prior is centred on no gap. The two intervals, however, differ in what they allow one to say, the confidence interval being a statement about the procedure, which covers the true gap in 95% of repeated studies, and the credible interval a statement about the gap itself, given the model, the prior and the data. The posterior answers questions that a confidence interval cannot, giving a probability of `r insight::format_value(orig_weak$pd, digits = 4)` that Hispanic names were greeted by name less often and a probability of `r insight::format_value(orig_weak$p_beyond_10, digits = 3)` that the gap exceeds 10 points in that direction.

Every number of this kind rests on the assumption that the computation worked. Stan draws from the posterior by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and the standard checks ask whether the four chains agree (the R-hat statistic, which should be below 1.01), whether the chains contain enough independent information (the effective sample sizes, which should exceed about 400) and whether the sampler entered regions that it could not explore (divergent transitions, which should be zero). @tbl-diagnostics reports these checks for every model on the page.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Computational checks of the eight models: the largest R-hat and the smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes of the coefficients, the divergent transitions and the deepest tree of the sampler, from 4 chains of 1,000 draws after warm-up. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_diagnostics.csv`."
#| echo: false
dx |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    Model = unname(c(prior_weak = "Prior only, weakly informative",
                     prior_sceptical = "Prior only, sceptical",
                     original_weak = "Original, weakly informative prior",
                     original_sceptical = "Original, sceptical prior",
                     replication_alone = "Replication, weakly informative prior",
                     replication_updated = "Replication, original posterior as prior",
                     joint_common = "Both studies, one gap",
                     joint_separate = "Both studies, a gap for each")[model]),
    `R-hat` = sprintf("%.3f", max_rhat),
    `Bulk ESS` = format(round(min_ess_bulk), big.mark = ","),
    `Tail ESS` = format(round(min_ess_tail), big.mark = ",")
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Model", "R-hat", "Bulk ESS", "Tail ESS", Divergences = "divergences",
                            `Tree depth` = "max_treedepth")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:6, align = "r")
```

## 4. What changes with the prior {#sec-sensitivity}

Under the sceptical prior the posterior median is `r insight::format_value(orig_scep$median, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, with a 95% credible interval from `r insight::format_value(orig_scep$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(orig_scep$q975, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`. The doubtful reader ends up nearly certain about which way the gap runs, with a probability of `r insight::format_value(orig_scep$pd, digits = 3)` that it is negative, but much less certain about its size, giving a gap beyond 10 points a probability of `r insight::format_value(orig_scep$p_beyond_10, digits = 2)`. @fig-sensitivity presents the two priors and the two posteriors side by side.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensitivity
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "The gap between Hispanic and white names in the original experiment under the two priors: the prior (dashed) and the posterior (solid) for each. The vertical line marks the reference specification of the course. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_draws.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Under the weakly informative prior the posterior is a hump centred near −19 points, far from its flat prior. Under the sceptical prior the posterior lies between the narrow prior at zero and the data, centred near −12 points."
draws |>
  datawizard::data_filter(quantity == "gap",
                          model %in% c("prior_weak", "prior_sceptical", "original_weak", "original_sceptical")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    prior = dplyr::if_else(grepl("weak", model), "weakly informative prior", "sceptical prior"),
    stage = dplyr::if_else(startsWith(model, "prior"), "prior", "posterior")
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(value, colour = prior, linetype = stage)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = ref$b_pp, colour = "grey45") +
  ggplot2::geom_density(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`weakly informative prior` = "#0e3b6a", `sceptical prior` = "#8c5a10"),
                               name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c(prior = "dashed", posterior = "solid"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-40, 20)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus white names (points)", y = "density") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Whereas a comparison of two fits answers the question for two priors, the priorsense package asks it for every prior close to the one chosen, without refitting the model. The package reweights the draws as if the prior, or the likelihood, had been raised to a power slightly above or below 1, and measures how far the posterior moves [@KallioinenEtAl2026PriorsenseEfficientPrior]. A posterior that moves with the prior but not with the likelihood is driven by the prior, while one that moves with both indicates that the prior and the data pull in different directions.

```{r}
#| label: priorsense
#| eval: false
priorsense::powerscale_sensitivity(fit_original, variable = "b_hisp")
```

For the weakly informative fit the sensitivity to the prior is `r insight::format_value(sens_weak$prior, digits = 3)` and to the likelihood `r insight::format_value(sens_weak$likelihood, digits = 3)`, against the default threshold of 0.05 used by the package, indicating that the posterior of the gap is determined by the data rather than by the prior. For the sceptical fit both values lie above the threshold, at `r insight::format_value(sens_scep$prior, digits = 3)` and `r insight::format_value(sens_scep$likelihood, digits = 3)`, and the package reports a "`r sens_scep$diagnosis`". The diagnosis is accurate, since the sceptical prior expects small gaps while the data hold a large one, and the posterior, being a compromise that depends on both, obliges anyone who reports it to defend the prior as well as the data. McElreath states the general point plainly: "the prior is considered to be just part of the model. As such it should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, p. 35].

## 5. The replication as new data {#sec-replication}

The replication supplies the external information that the sceptical prior lacked, and Bayesian estimation offers two ways of using it. The first is sequential, with the posterior from the original experiment becoming the prior for the replication. "When you have a previous estimate to provide to the machine, that can become the prior", as McElreath describes the updating of a model, in which "each estimate becomes the prior for the next step" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, p. 34]. The script carries the posterior of the coefficient, summarised by its mean and standard deviation, into a normal prior for the gap in the replication, an approximation that is close for a log-odds coefficient estimated from several hundred replies. The intercept retains the weakly informative prior, since the replication used new names in another year and the share of greetings for its white names need not match that of the original.

```{r}
#| label: brms-update
#| eval: false
carried <- posterior::summarise_draws(brms::as_draws_df(fit_original, variable = "b_hisp"), "mean", "sd")
fit_updated <- brms::brm(
  k | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + hisp, family = stats::binomial(),
  data = datawizard::data_filter(counts, study == "replication"),
  prior = c(brms::prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
            brms::set_prior(sprintf("normal(%.4f, %.4f)", carried$mean, carried$sd), class = "b", coef = "hisp")),
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 20261105, backend = "cmdstanr"
)
```

The second route places both studies in one model, with a share of greetings for the white names in each study and a single gap on the log-odds scale (`k | trials(n) ~ 0 + study + hisp`). The two routes rest on the same assumption, that the two experiments measure one gap, and arrive at nearly the same answer. On its own the replication yields a gap of `r insight::format_value(round(repl_alone$median, 1), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points (95% credible interval `r insight::format_value(repl_alone$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to +`r insight::format_value(repl_alone$q975, digits = 1)`). With the original posterior as its prior the gap is `r insight::format_value(repl_upd$median, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points (`r insight::format_value(repl_upd$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to +`r insight::format_value(repl_upd$q975, digits = 1)`), and in the joint model, expressed at the share for the original white names, `r insight::format_value(joint_orig$median, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points (`r insight::format_value(joint_orig$q025, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to +`r insight::format_value(joint_orig$q975, digits = 1)`). The arithmetic behind this agreement is explained in *Regression and Other Stories*, according to which, in the simplest case, the Bayesian estimate is "a weighted average of prior and data estimates, where each estimate gets a weight proportional to the inverse square of its standard error", a rule resting on "the key assumption ... that the prior and data represent two different sources of information" [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories, pp. 119–120]. Since the replication has about four times as many replies as the original experiment, it carries most of the weight.

```{r}
#| label: fig-update
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "The posterior distributions of the gap from the original experiment alone, from the replication alone (both with the weakly informative prior), and from the replication with the posterior of the original as its prior. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing_draws.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Three densities. The original experiment lies around −19 points and is wide; the replication alone is a narrow peak around zero; the combined posterior lies between them, around −4 points, and is the narrowest."
draws |>
  datawizard::data_filter(quantity == "gap", model %in% c("original_weak", "replication_alone", "replication_updated")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(result = factor(model, levels = c("original_weak", "replication_alone", "replication_updated"),
                                          labels = c("original experiment", "replication alone", "replication, original as prior"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(value, colour = result)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  ggplot2::geom_density(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`original experiment` = "#0e3b6a", `replication alone` = "#8c5a10",
                                          `replication, original as prior` = "#8b1538"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-40, 15)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in greetings by name, Hispanic minus white names (points)", y = "posterior density") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

The combined posterior is narrower than either of the other two and lies where neither study put its estimate, which is a reason to check the assumption before reading the combined result. For the updated model priorsense reports a "`r sens_upd$diagnosis`" (sensitivity to the prior `r insight::format_value(sens_upd$prior, digits = 3)`, to the likelihood `r insight::format_value(sens_upd$likelihood, digits = 3)`), indicating that the posterior from the original experiment and the data from the replication pull in different directions. A posterior predictive check of the joint model points the same way in terms of the data. Replicated from the fitted model, the share of greetings for the white names in the original experiment has a 90% interval from `r insight::format_value(ppc_common$rep_q05[ppc_common$hisp == 0], digits = 1)`% to `r insight::format_value(ppc_common$rep_q95[ppc_common$hisp == 0], digits = 1)`%, and the observed share, `r insight::format_value(ppc_common$observed[ppc_common$hisp == 0], digits = 1)`%, lies outside this interval, while the observed `r insight::format_value(ppc_common$observed[ppc_common$hisp == 1], digits = 1)`% for the Hispanic names lies just below its own interval, which starts at `r insight::format_value(ppc_common$rep_q05[ppc_common$hisp == 1], digits = 1)`%. A model with one gap is unable to reproduce the original experiment, and the failed check names the next model, one with a gap for each study (`k | trials(n) ~ 0 + study + study:hisp`). In that model the replication gap exceeds the original gap by `r insight::format_value(joint_diff$median, digits = 1)` points, with a 95% credible interval from `r insight::format_value(joint_diff$q025, digits = 1)` to `r insight::format_value(joint_diff$q975, digits = 1)`. The two studies, in other words, disagree, and the combined estimate of about four points describes neither of them. The same conclusion is reached with the tools of meta-analysis in the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-two-studies), which also asks what weight a pooled estimate of two studies can bear.

## 6. Type S and type M errors {#sec-design}

The disagreement between the two studies may have many sources, among them the names, the authorities and the six years separating the two experiments, and one of these sources can be assessed with the numbers of the case study alone, namely how a study as large as the original behaves when the true gap is small. @GelmanCarlin2014PowerCalculationsAssessing propose a design analysis that reports, beside the power, two errors of a significant result. The type S error rate is "the probability that the replicated estimate has the incorrect sign, if it is statistically significantly different from zero", and the exaggeration ratio, or expected type M error, is "the expectation of the absolute value of the estimate divided by the effect size, if statistically significantly different from zero" (p. 643). The calculation requires the standard error of the study and a true effect, and Gelman and Carlin insist that the true effect come from outside the study: "Design calculations, whether prospective or retrospective, should be based on realistic external estimates of effect sizes" (p. 642). For the original experiment such an estimate is supplied by the replication, and section 5 put the gap at about four points once both studies are counted. The retrodesign package, written from the function published in the article by Gelman and Carlin, computes the three quantities for several true gaps, at the standard error of the reference comparison in the original study and at that of the replication.

```{r}
#| label: retrodesign
# The closed form of Lu et al. (2018), cited on the help page of retrodesign,
# for a normal sampling distribution; retrodesign::retrodesign() simulates a t
design <- tidyr::expand_grid(study = c("original", "replication"), true_gap = c(2, 4, 10, 20)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(se = dplyr::if_else(study == "original", ref$se_pp, repl_row$se_pp),
                result = purrr::map2(true_gap, se, \(a, s) retrodesign::retro_design_closed_form(a, s))) |>
  tidyr::unnest_wider(result)
design |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.double), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: design-values
#| include: false
d_orig <- design |> datawizard::data_filter(study == "original")
d_repl <- design |> datawizard::data_filter(study == "replication")
```

With a standard error of `r insight::format_value(ref$se_pp, digits = 2)` points, the original comparison has a power of `r insight::format_value(d_orig$power[2], digits = 2)` if the true gap is 4 points. A significant estimate would then carry the wrong sign with a probability of `r insight::format_value(d_orig$type_s[2], digits = 3)` and, when in the right direction, would exaggerate the true gap by a factor of `r insight::format_value(d_orig$type_m[2], digits = 1)` on average, which means that a significant estimate of about `r insight::format_value(4 * d_orig$type_m[2], digits = 0)` points is what a study of this size produces when the gap is about 4. At a true gap of 2 points the exaggeration ratio is `r insight::format_value(d_orig$type_m[1], digits = 1)`, and only at 20 points does it approach 1 (`r insight::format_value(d_orig$type_m[4], digits = 2)`). The replication, with a standard error of `r insight::format_value(repl_row$se_pp, digits = 2)` points, exaggerates a true gap of 10 points by a factor of `r insight::format_value(d_repl$type_m[3], digits = 2)` and a gap of 4 points by a factor of `r insight::format_value(d_repl$type_m[2], digits = 1)`. Gelman and Carlin note that "[p]roblems with the exaggeration ratio start to arise when power is less than 0.5, and problems with the Type S error rate start to arise when power is less than 0.1" (pp. 643–644), and the original comparison falls below the first of these thresholds for any true gap smaller than about 10 points. The power curves of the two studies are drawn in the [experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-power), which also computes the exaggeration at a true gap of 10 points and counts the same exaggeration in simulated experiments.

None of these calculations shows that the original estimate is exaggerated. If the true gap were about 4 points, the original design would reach significance about one time in eight, its significant estimates would average about `r insight::format_value(4 * d_orig$type_m[2], digits = 0)` points, and an estimate as large as 20 points would be rare even among these significant estimates, which suggests that the filter of significance alone does not explain the published gap. What the design analysis does show is that a significant result from a study of this size says little about the size of the gap, since any gap below about 10 points that reached significance would have been reported as one of 10 points or more. The replication places the gap in 2020 close to zero, and since the names, the authorities and the year all changed between the two studies, the case-study data cannot establish how much of the difference between the studies is attributable to chance and how much to these changes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the sceptical prior to normal(0, 0.5), the prior that McElreath uses for treatment effects in a logistic regression (p. 329), and work out what it implies for the gap in points: simulate 4,000 draws with `stats::rnorm()` for the intercept and the gap, convert them with `stats::plogis()`, and take the difference. Then run `retrodesign::retro_design_closed_form()` at the standard error of the original comparison for the posterior median of the joint model, `r insight::format_value(abs(joint_orig$median), digits = 1)` points, and write two sentences on what the result says about the published gap.
:::

## Further reading {#sec-further}

For readers learning Bayesian estimation from the start, *Statistical Rethinking* builds it up from counting and simulation, with priors chosen by prior predictive simulation throughout [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian], while *Regression and Other Stories* treats regression with the same habits and with weakly informative priors as the default [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories]. *Bayesian Data Analysis* is the reference text, covering also the hierarchical models that combine several studies [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis], and the *Bayesian Workflow* book describes the cycle of building, checking and revising a model followed in miniature on this page, from the prior predictive check to the posterior predictive check that names the next model [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow]. The design analysis of section 6 comes from @GelmanCarlin2014PowerCalculationsAssessing, while the models are fitted with brms [@Burkner2017BrmsPackageBayesian], the gaps in points are computed with marginaleffects [@Arel-BundockEtAl2024HowInterpretStatistical] and the sensitivity checks with priorsense [@KallioinenEtAl2026PriorsenseEfficientPrior]. Every model on the page is fitted by the script `companion/_model-outputs/bayes_housing.R`, whose outputs are listed in `companion/_model-outputs/manifest.txt`.
